Fisher Scoring, With Its Own Settings

Source: R/fisher_scoring.R
fisher_scoring.Rd

Returns a specification of Fisher scoring for fit_distrib()'s method argument. The specification records how the expected information is obtained, and optionally a stopping rule and an iteration limit of its own. It is fit_distrib()'s default method.

Fisher scoring is Newton's method in which the observed Hessian is replaced by minus the expected information, so it needs no implementation of its own and is not an optimizer. It needs one thing for which an optimizer has no slot, the statement of how that matrix is obtained, and this object holds that statement.

Usage

fisher_scoring(method = NULL, criterion = NULL, maxit = NULL)

Arguments

method

NULL (the default) or an object that selects how the expected information is obtained:

  • NULL: the closed form of the family where it has one, and expect_opg() otherwise;

  • expect_opg(): the outer product of the observed scores, which costs one gradient;

  • expect_integrate(): quadrature (or summation over the support) of the observed Hessian with identity = "hessian", or of minus the outer product of the scores with identity = "score";

  • expect_mc(): Monte Carlo, with the sample size nsim and the identity set in that constructor.

Any other value, a character string included, signals an error. expected_derivative_methods compares the methods.

criterion

A stopping rule from optimizers7, or NULL (the default), in which case fit_distrib() stops on optimizers7::crit_grad() at its default tolerance. An object that is not a criterion signals an error.

maxit

An iteration limit, a single number at least 1, or NULL (the default) for the limit of optimizers7::newton(). When the limit is reached the fit reports converged = FALSE and keeps the point.

Value

An S7 object of class FisherScoring(), with properties method (NULL or an object inheriting from ExpectMethod), criterion and maxit.

Values accepted by the method argument

fit_distrib() has one argument that selects how to optimize, and that argument accepts an optimizer of optimizers7 or this object:

method = fisher_scoring()Newton's method with the expected information
method = optimizers7::newton()Newton's method with the observed Hessian
method = optimizers7::lbfgs()whatever that optimizer does

The step

Writing \(s(\eta) = \partial \ell / \partial \eta\) for the score on the unconstrained scale and \(\mathcal{I}(\eta) = \mathbb{E}[-\partial^{2} \ell / \partial \eta \partial \eta']\) for the expected information there, the step is $$\eta^{(t+1)} = \eta^{(t)} + \mathcal{I}(\eta^{(t)})^{-1} s(\eta^{(t)}).$$ Under the diagonal reparametrization \(\theta_i = h_i(\eta_i)\) the information transforms by congruence, \(\mathcal{I}(\eta) = D\,\mathcal{I}(\theta)\,D\) with \(D = \operatorname{diag}(h_i'(\eta_i))\), and the first-order term of the chain rule vanishes in expectation because the score has mean zero. The matrix inverted is therefore positive definite wherever \(\mathcal{I}(\theta)\) is, and the step is a direction of ascent. A fit therefore succeeds on a family whose observed Hessian is indefinite; the Laplace is the standard case.

Methods for the expected information

With method = NULL, the default, the fit takes the closed form of the expected information where the family has one, and the outer product of the observed scores (expect_opg()) otherwise, as for a family defined by its density alone or a truncated family. An object selects the method for every family, including a family that has the closed form: the fit then uses the expectation as that method computes it, and the closed form is not read. The methods differ in cost and in variance: expect_opg() costs one gradient, expect_integrate() is deterministic and dearer, and expect_mc() adds simulation noise that decreases with its nsim. expected_derivative_methods compares them.

See also

fit_distrib(), which consumes this; FisherScoring() for the class; expected_derivative_methods for what each method computes; distrib_expected_hessian() for the matrix itself; optimizers7::newton(), whose iteration limit stands where this sets none.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- gaussian1_distrib()
y <- distrib_rng(d, 100, list(mu = 1, sigma = 2))

# The default and the explicit specification give the same fit.
coef(fit_distrib(d, y))
#>       mu    sigma 
#> 1.217775 1.787394 
coef(fit_distrib(d, y, method = fisher_scoring()))
#>       mu    sigma 
#> 1.217775 1.787394 

# The step rests on a congruence: the information on the link scale is
# D I(theta) D, with D the diagonal of the inverse link's derivative.
th <- list(mu = 1, sigma = 2)
It <- distrib_expected_hessian(d, y, th)
Ie <- distrib_expected_hessian(d, y, th, scale = "link")
c(theta = sum(It$sigma_sigma), link = sum(Ie$sigma_sigma))   # ratio 2^2
#> theta  link 
#>   -50  -200 

# An object in 'method' is used also by a family that has a closed form:
# here the expected information is simulated, and the fit stays close to the
# one that uses the closed form.
set.seed(2)
coef(fit_distrib(d, y, method = fisher_scoring(method = expect_mc(nsim = 2000))))
#>       mu    sigma 
#> 1.217775 1.787394 

# The stopping rule and the budget belong to the method.
fit <- fit_distrib(d, y, method = fisher_scoring(maxit = 1))
c(iterations = fit@iterations, converged = fit@converged)
#> iterations  converged 
#>          1          0
